title: Nathan Fielder made a secret documentary about Elizabeth Holmes
author: Matty Merritt
content: Culture Nathan Fielder made a secret documentary about Elizabeth Holmes It’s apparently really weird. By Matty Merritt September 8, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: Culture / Arts, Performance & Institutions / Film & Cinema A new documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes will hit theaters in October, but don’t expect to leave with any clear answers. And before the trailer for You Can See Everything dropped yesterday alongside its buzzy premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, basically no one knew it existed. It’s apparently really weird. In 2023, just 36 days before starting her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors by lying about her company’s blood-testing machines, Holmes allowed Fielder and his crew to shoot a documentary in her home. Fielder even lived with Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans (and their two kids), for a few days: The filming took place in secret. The audience at Telluride didn’t even know what the movie was about until they entered the theater. Throughout the doc, which runs almost three hours, Fielder tries to find the truth about what happened with Theranos and if Holmes was being manipulated—or doing the manipulating. There are apparently twists. If you think Holmes’s story has already been detailed to death in longform articles, a book, podcasts, and a Hulu series, reviewers say you’re wrong. Fielder said in a post-film Q&A, “I really am struggling to this day to understand exactly what I experienced.” And many of those at the Telluride screening said it’s unlike anything they’ve ever watched.— MM Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: Labor Day gas prices have never been this high
author: Molly Liebergall
description: Gas never surpassed $4/gallon on Labor Day before this year.
content: US Economy Labor Day gas prices have never been this high Gas never surpassed $4/gallon on Labor Day before this year. By Molly Liebergall September 8, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: US Economy / Inflation, Prices & Cost of Living / Energy Prices & Fuel Costs Credit cards were working overtime at gas stations across the US this weekend. Pump prices for this time of year hit their highest level on record over the holiday, driven by continued oil disruptions from the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war. Gas cost an average of $4.15 per gallon yesterday, according to AAA: Gas never surpassed $4/gallon on Labor Day before this year. The previous record for the holiday was $3.82/gallon, set in 2012 (the record is $5.02/gallon in June 2022). The new record is ~30% higher than gas prices were this time last year, on average. For context, gas prices tend to move seasonally—rising through spring and summer, beginning their descent by Labor Day, and hitting their lowest lows in the winter, when days are shorter and people tend to drive less. This year is an exception: Iran has constrained tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz since the war started in February, while Ukrainian drone attacks have disabled some Russian refineries. US gas inventories were 6% below average for the last full week of August, according to the US Energy Information Administration. You’re still feeling the effects, even if you don’t have a car According to AAA: Diesel (fuel for freight trucks that carry everything from food to clothing) spiked almost 60% from last Labor Day weekend to hit a record high of $5.85/gallon going into the holiday. Prices for domestic flights to 10 of the most popular US destinations were up ~20% this weekend compared with last year. Looking ahead… the EPA moved up the date when refineries can switch from summer gas blends to cheaper winter blends from Sept. 15 to Sept. 1, which may provide some relief at the pump. But the broader oil outlook is uncertain: Iran plans to expand its Strait lockdown in response to new US strikes, and US refineries are already working at near-total capacity. —ML Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: The facilities are getting fancy
author: Sam Klebanov
description: One facility owner told Bloomberg that youth sports buildings are “recession-proof,” since spending on the dream of their kids going pro is among the last things parents will cut back on.
content: Real Estate The facilities are getting fancy One facility owner told Bloomberg that youth sports buildings are “recession-proof,” since spending on the dream of their kids going pro is among the last things parents will cut back on. By Sam Klebanov September 6, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: Real Estate / Commercial Real Estate / Mixed-Use Development Many young athletes today aren’t forced to do drills on the steps of their local art museum. That’s because real estate developers are going all in on the youth sports boom by building state-of-the-art training grounds that Rocky would envy. One facility owner told Bloomberg that youth sports buildings are “recession-proof,” since parents spending on the dream of their kids going pro is among the last things they will cut back on. Here are just a few places where children train like elite athletes: The Program NYC is a 12,500-square-foot basketball training center for players 6 and older in Brooklyn offering weight training and recovery amenities, including a sauna, cold plunge, and air compression massage. Youth Membership costs $500 per month or $4,500 for an annual commitment. It also offers the Platinum Membership, a “basketball concierge service for the Middle, High School, College or Pro player looking to to take the next step in his/her basketball journey,” for $2,500 per month. The growing bougie basketball court chain Shoot360 has 50 locations worldwide, offering AI-enabled training with instant analytic feedback. Travel baseball teams at the Ballparks of America in Missouri play in replicas of famous MLB stadiums and stay in on-site dorms. The $125 million AdventHealth Sports Park in Kansas opened in 2024 with an NHL-regulation ice rink, basketball courts that convert to accommodate pickleball or volleyball, and a recovery center with a hydrotherapy pool. The $60 million Eagle Stadium in Allen, TX, (pictured above) has 18,000 seats, a jumbotron, a weightlifting room, and a luxury suite for VIP spectators. It serves as the home field for a local high school football team. The upshot: Athletics administrators told Bloomberg that the pricey private facilities are sprouting up amid disinvestment from free public courts and fields, making sports participation less affordable. —SK Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: Girls flag football is on a remarkable a run
author: Brendan Cosgrove
description: It’s one of the fastest-growing sports in the US, especially at the high school level.
content: Sports Girls flag football is on a remarkable a run It’s one of the fastest-growing sports in the US, especially at the high school level. By Brendan Cosgrove September 6, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: Sports / Recreational Sports / Youth Sports Industry Girls flag football is a hit. Not literally, of course, since it doesn’t allow tackling. But it’s one of the fastest-growing sports in the US, especially at the high school level. According to a survey conducted by the National Federation of State High School Associations: Around 102,000 high school girls participated in flag football last year—up from less than 16,000 four years earlier. The number of schools reporting participation went from 2,736 last year to 3,990 this year. The little ones are playing, too. The number of girls age 6 to 12 playing flag football increased by 283% between 2015 and 2024, according to USA Football. Meanwhile, about 500,000 girls age 6 to 17 play on organized flag football teams in the US, per the Arthur M. Blank Family Foundation, which has partnered with the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons (of which Blank is majority owner) to champion the sport’s growth . Green flag: According to Amanda Dinkel, the Falcons’ senior director for community relations, flag football “provides gender equality and builds girls’ leadership skills…and 50% of the girls who decide to play flag have never played a sport before.” Flags of the world: The NFL estimates that more than 20 million people play flag football in 100+ countries. The sport will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles in 2028.— BC Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: Has youth sports lost the plot?
author: Molly Liebergall
description: Over the past two decades, private equity has transformed youth sports into an industrial complex that’s cutthroat enough to cause a shortage of willing umpires and referees, and expensive enough to break the bank.
content: Sports Has youth sports lost the plot? Over the past two decades, private equity has transformed youth sports into an industrial complex that’s cutthroat enough to cause a shortage of willing umpires and referees, and expensive enough to break the bank. By Molly Liebergall September 6, 2026 • 3 min read TOPICS: Sports / Recreational Sports / Youth Sports Industry When news broke that Kim Kardashian would produce a TV show following the parents of elite teen baseball players, the internet’s broad reaction was: This is the last thing kids need right now. Over the past two decades, private equity has transformed youth sports into an industrial complex that’s cutthroat enough to cause a shortage of willing umpires and referees, and expensive enough to break the bank. Case study: One Florida parent who recalls playing rec sports for $80 per season as a child now spends $8,000 per year on her 12-year-old son’s club baseball practices, tournaments, and equipment, she told the Washington Post. She’s in good company: Family spending on youth sports leaped by 46% from 2019 to 2024 to make it a $40 billion-a-year industry—more than the combined annual revenue of the NFL and NBA, according to the Aspen Institute. Financial strain has caused 1 in 5 parents to limit or end their kids’ participation in youth sports, according to a New York Life survey from last year. How did we get here? When parks and recreation departments suffered budget cuts after the 2008 financial crisis and again during the pandemic, it exacerbated longstanding public funding issues and left gaps for investors to plug. And private equity has been on a spree—snatching up teams, facilities, software, training camps, apparel, and media rights. Major PE-funded entities include: Black Bear Sports Group, the nation’s largest hockey rink owner-operator, which charges up to $37 per month to stream kids’ games, and prohibits parents from livestreaming or broadcasting the matches themselves. Varsity Brands, the KKR-owned cheerleading and sports apparel behemoth that ballooned in valuation from $1.5 billion in 2014 to $4.5 billion in 2024—the same year it settled anticompetitive allegations for $82.5 million. Unrivaled Sports, a new venture from the owner of the NFL’s Washington Commanders that seeks to dominate the burgeoning youth flag football space. The promise of PE-funded leagues is that they’ll help turn your kid into the next Cristiano Ronaldo or Paige Bueckers, but there’s little evidence to support this. In fact, some studies suggest that sports specialization at a young age increases an athlete’s risk of injuries into adulthood. Nonetheless, parents who want their kids to excel on the field increasingly feel like they don’t have a choice but to opt for pay-to-play leagues that start stealing players from community teams as early as kindergarten. Looking ahead… youth sports privatization could be a 2028 election issue. Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy—identified by The Atlantic as a potential Democratic presidential nominee—is pushing a bill that would limit private equity’s place in kids’ sports. —ML Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: There’s surprising good news about the job market
author: Sam Klebanov
description: The US added 162,000 jobs in August, vastly exceeding the employment growth economists expected.
content: US Economy There’s surprising good news about the job market The US added 162,000 jobs in August, vastly exceeding the employment growth economists expected. By Sam Klebanov September 5, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: US Economy / Labor Markets / Jobs Reports August blindsided everyone, and not just by how fast summer ended: The US added 162,000 jobs last month, according to government data released yesterday. That’s more than triple the number that economists polled by Dow Jones predicted. Plus, the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%, and the share of Americans who gave up on looking for work or worked part time due to a lack of full-time options dropped slightly. Unlike in prior months, the job gains weren’t mostly in healthcare: Restaurants and bars added 59,000 workers. Construction and manufacturing payrolls grew by 22,000 and 16,000, respectively, while public schools gained 42,000 employees, rebounding from July’s decline. But the information sector—which includes tech jobs—shed 23,000 workers, which some analysts said could reflect AI automating white-collar work. Overall: After job growth was revised upward by a total of 55,000 for the previous two months, the US added an average of 80,000 jobs monthly so far in 2026—an improvement from less than 10,000 per month last year, but below the pace of hiring in 2023 and 2024. It’s not all rosy: Inflation outpaced the yearly wage growth, which slowed to 3.1%, down from 3.7% pay growth a year ago. Stronger case to hike interest rates Analysts say that now that the job market looks healthier, the Fed will focus on inflation data due next week as it mulls whether to hike interest rates at its next meeting on Sept. 16. Wall Street thinks a rate hike has become more likely: The trading odds of a rate hike increased from 49% to 59% yesterday. The 2-year Treasury bond yield—which is closely correlated with the interest rates the Fed sets—also rose yesterday. But President Trump issued a blistering threat… that if the Fed doesn’t react to the employment rebound by slashing interest rates, he’ll end trade with nations that have a trade deficit with the US—a long list that includes the EU and China. —SK Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: PBR wants your help finding $70k of stolen beer
author: Molly Liebergall
description: “Kudos to them, perhaps. I’m sure they look cool with a garage full of PBR,” Pabst CEO Greig DeBow said in a TikTok post announcing the bounty and asking the thieves to return the beer.
content: Lifestyle PBR wants your help finding $70k of stolen beer “Kudos to them, perhaps. I’m sure they look cool with a garage full of PBR,” Pabst CEO Greig DeBow said in a TikTok post announcing the bounty and asking the thieves to return the beer. By Molly Liebergall September 5, 2026 • less than 3 min read TOPICS: Lifestyle / Food & Drink / Coffee & Beverages Pabst Blue Ribbon is using a recent beer heist to tap into the zeitgeist. This week, the lager-maker spun a theft of its cargo into a marketing campaign, offering up to $20,000 as a reward for information that helps track down a frat house’s worth of beer that got snatched last month. ICYMI: In two back-to-back swipes, brewski thieves stole more than 1,500 cases of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer—snagging a total of approximately 34,000 cans, worth ~$70,000—from a Southern California warehouse. One shipment of beer vanished en route to Arizona, while another was picked up by a group that forged documents to pose as a subcontracting company, according to local police. “Kudos to them, perhaps. I’m sure they look cool with a garage full of PBR,” Pabst CEO Greig DeBow said in a TikTok post announcing the bounty and asking the thieves to return the beer. Pabst has posted several times since getting its cans pilfered to lightheartedly ask the public to keep its eyes peeled for a “ missing truck .” Getting robbed is the hot new marketing campaign: PBR is following in the footsteps of KitKat, which similarly capitalized with social media posts and even a “Stolen KitKat Tracker” after thieves snagged 400,000+ candy bars earlier this year. The campaign earned a Cannes Lions trophy this summer. —ML Copy Become smarter in just 5 minutes Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley. title: How whole life insurance plays a role in your financial portfolio
author: Morning Brew Creative Studio
description: Whole life insurance isn’t just a policy to take care of your loved ones. It can also be an asset in your wider portfolio.
content: TOGETHER WITH Finance Rethinking your portfolio: Life insurance’s role in a long-term strategy Whole life insurance isn’t just a policy to take care of your loved ones. It can also be an asset in your wider portfolio. By Morning Brew Creative Studio September 4, 2026 • 4 min read TOPICS: Finance / Personal Finance / Budgeting & Savings Trends TOGETHER WITH Protect what matters. For savvy investors at all career levels and life stages, incorporating life insurance into their financial strategy can help round out financial plans and protect what they’ve created. At New York Life, financial professionals help you build a personalized, long-term strategy that evolves alongside your life. Get started . You’ve built a well-rounded portfolio that can support you and your family. Now what? It’s time to think about life insurance. No, we’re not catastrophizing. Whole life insurance can be more than protection for your loved ones should something unexpected happen. It may be another piece in the wider puzzle of your portfolio. Rather than viewing life insurance as an isolated asset separate from savings and investments, consider how it can complement a broader financial strategy. Whole life insurance can bring protection and cash-value growth together to support long-term goals. Whole life insurance isn’t exclusive to folks who are just starting to think about retirement, either. Savvy investors at all career levels and life stages may benefit from adding life insurance to their portfolios if they have protection needs. By establishing a diversified, goal-based financial foundation, you can help protect your loved ones’ futures from market uncertainty, inflation, and other external risks. After all, your portfolio can’t rely on returns alone. You need protection, growth, and gains to work together . We teamed up with New York Life to learn about the role life insurance plays in your portfolio, how it works alongside your existing assets, and how it interacts with complex financial goals. Let’s get started. Starting early It’s not cliché to say that it’s never too early to start planning for your financial future. For young, affluent professionals, financial success isn’t the accumulation of assets. Instead, they view success as building a healthy financial infrastructure that can protect them as they grow. Creating a strong, well-rounded portfolio in early career stages helps support future goals and responsibilities alike. As young professionals’ careers, families, and responsibilities evolve, their financial planning becomes more interconnected and, well, complicated. Put simply, they may not want to rely on investments alone. By adding that third bucket of protection to their financial portfolios, young professionals can help reduce their reliance on just one category. They can create a steady base that weathers market downturns, unexpected life events, and anything else thrown their way. Steady and stable It’s impossible to know for certain what’s waiting around the corner, and predicting what could happen is just as difficult. With life insurance, individuals can prepare—as much as is possible—for the unexpected. Behavioral economist Shlomo Benartzi has written about the importance of considering protection and growth together rather than as separate financial decisions. That’s where life insurance comes in. Life insurance can help stabilize a wider financial plan when it works in tandem with savings and investment strategies. That being said, it can’t replace savings or investments, and it can’t work alone. Life insurance can complement the other aspects of a financial plan. As financial situations become more complex, life insurance serves as more than a safety net. As individuals expand their families, buy homes, take new steps in their careers, and try new things, it’s more important than ever that they create a plan. Life insurance becomes an important tool to help them build confidence in their future while protecting the things that matter most. Protect what matters most Building a strong financial foundation starts with seeking trusted guidance from a financial professional. They focus on more than life insurance and work with individuals to understand their goals. By taking a long-term view, New York Life professionals help clients build financial strategies designed to evolve with them as their lives, priorities, and financial needs change. Planning ahead No matter where you are in your life or career, now is the perfect time to plan for your financial future.
